article.overview: The Fuel cell experiment is a lunar technology entry in the catalogue's category of lunar technology and infrastructure experiments. A fuel cell converts stored hydrogen and oxygen into electricity and water. In a regenerative configuration, an electrolyser uses surplus electricity to split the water back into hydrogen and oxygen, so the same system can store energy and release it later. The catalogue does not identify one flown lunar instrument with this name. This article therefore covers the concept and the documented examples, and separates hardware that has flown from ground development, studies and press-reported testing. The most significant flown precedent is the set of fuel cell power plants that supplied electricity to the Apollo command and service modules. Those were spacecraft power subsystems rather than standalone experiments.
article.description: A fuel cell is an electrochemical device. Hydrogen is supplied to one electrode and oxygen to the other. An electrolyte allows ions to pass between the electrodes while electrons are forced through an external circuit, which provides electric current. The by-products are water and heat. Two broad designs are relevant. Alkaline fuel cells, which NASA describes as the type used in the Apollo and Space Shuttle programmes [2], use a liquid alkaline electrolyte. Proton exchange membrane (PEM) cells, used in several of the development efforts described below, use a solid polymer membrane. In a lunar application the reactants must be stored in tanks, and the water produced must be managed. A regenerative fuel cell system adds an electrolyser that uses solar electricity during the lunar day to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. These gases are stored and later recombined at night [4][5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar fuel cell system is to provide electrical power and, in regenerative designs, energy storage for periods when solar power is unavailable. The lunar night lasts about two weeks, so a solar-powered surface asset must either store energy or stop operating [5]. Fuel cells have also been valued for their energy per unit mass. NASA states that during the Apollo programme fuel cells offered more energy per pound than batteries could over the course of a long mission [1]. Regenerative systems also produce water that can be recycled. A trade-press report links one development effort to Artemis lunar life-support readiness [6]. Applications therefore include surface power storage, power for crewed missions and possible water or life-support co-benefits. The evidence for the last category is limited to press statements, not to verified system requirements.
article.operating_principle: In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode, releasing electrons that travel through an external load. Oxygen is reduced at the cathode and combines with hydrogen ions and electrons to form water. A single cell produces a low voltage, so many cells are connected in series to give a useful output voltage. Apollo service module fuel cells were built this way: each Apollo unit contained 31 separate but connected cells [3]. Regenerative operation reverses the process in an electrolyser. The ESA article describes a closed loop in which solar power splits water into hydrogen and oxygen by day, the gases are stored, and the fuel cell operates at night to produce power, water and heat, with the water recycled [4]. Honda's described approach is similar. Hydrogen is stored during the lunar day and converted back to electricity at night, and the water is fed to a high-pressure electrolysis system [5]. Neither the ESA article nor the Honda study article states the electrochemistry of the Honda system.
article.scientific_importance: The entry is primarily an engineering-enabling technology rather than a scientific instrument. Its scientific relevance is indirect. Reliable lunar-night power would allow longer surface experiments, continuous operation of sensors and communications, and sustained observation of surface processes. The Apollo fuel cell flights showed that hydrogen-oxygen electrochemical power could be used in crewed spacecraft [1][3]. Regenerative systems are at an earlier stage. Their scientific value depends on demonstrated round-trip efficiency, mass, lifetime and reliability in lunar conditions. The sources reviewed for this article do not provide those values for any regenerative lunar system.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a fuel cell energy system, and the catalogue entry does not define one. The examples below describe Apollo-era flight hardware and several development efforts. Where a mass, dimension, power or efficiency value was not found in a clearly identified source, it is recorded as not publicly specified rather than estimated. Figures apply only to the example in which they appear and should not be compared directly across examples, because the designs differ in chemistry, purpose, scale and maturity.

examples.name: Apollo command and service module fuel cell power plants
examples.summary: Three fuel cell power plants were installed in the Apollo service module and supplied electricity for the capsule carrying the astronauts [1]. Each fuel cell contained 31 separate but connected cells [3]. The cells are described as alkaline [2]. Hydrogen and oxygen were stored in tanks in the service module [3]. The mass, dimensions, power output and efficiency of the flight units were not verified against a primary technical document in this review, so those values are recorded as null in the JSON file. Apollo 13 illustrates the dependence on shared reactant storage. Readouts indicated that the oxygen tank and fuel cells 1 and 3 had failed, while fuel cell 2 continued to function [3]. Mission rules at the time stated that a lunar landing could not be made with two fuel cells [3].

examples.name: ESA closed-loop regenerative fuel cell system
examples.type: Ground development (regenerative PEM fuel cell and electrolyser)
examples.summary: ESA reports a closed-loop regenerative fuel cell system developed under a Greek-funded programme and led by Advent Technologies SA, with partners CERTH, FORTH and the University of Patras [4]. The article says the system demonstrated operational capability and that its fuel cell and electrolyser stacks reached 'TLR 5' (sic, as written in the article) [4]. It also describes regenerative PEM technology as exceeding TRL 4 [4]. The article is an archive item dated 3 February 2023. It does not name a flight, a test location or a lunar mission [4]. Its only numerical comparison states that the system's specific energy is 'more than double' the 200 Wh/kg of space-capable lithium-ion batteries. No measured specific energy value is given [4]. ESA suggests the technology could be scaled up to support the European Argonaut lunar lander. This is a proposed application, not a verified interface [4]. Power, energy capacity, mass, volume and round-trip efficiency are not publicly specified in the source.

key_values.tech_readiness_as_stated: TLR 5 (sic) for the fuel cell and electrolyser stacks; regenerative PEM technology exceeds TRL 4

examples.name: Honda regenerative fuel cell and Astrobotic LunaGrid study
examples.status: study under a joint development agreement; no flight date
examples.summary: Honda and Astrobotic announced a joint development agreement in September 2025 to study whether Honda's regenerative fuel cell could be integrated with Astrobotic's LunaGrid, a solar-array-based power service [5]. The study covers illumination analysis, scalability and hardware and software integration [5]. The sites considered are not specified in this article. The reported Astrobotic solar array capacity of 'up to 10 kilowatts' is a solar array figure, not a fuel cell specification [5]. The article gives no power, energy storage, mass or electrochemistry data for the Honda system and does not state a flight date [5]. Any flight or lunar-surface demonstration remains a proposal.

key_values.associated_solar_array_capacity_as_state: up to 10 kW (Astrobotic VSAT solar array, planned)

examples.name: Nimbus Power Systems PEM fuel cell stack tested with Blue Origin
examples.type: Qualification testing reported in trade press
examples.status: ground testing reported; no flight confirmed
examples.summary: A trade-press article dated 15 January 2026 reports that Nimbus Power Systems and Blue Origin tested a gravity-independent PEM fuel cell stack under launch-like vibration and shock conditions [6]. The article body available to this review was truncated, and no quantitative results were visible [6]. The article associates the work with Artemis lunar life-support readiness. It does not confirm a flight, a lander integration or a zero-gravity test [6]. Because this is a secondary source and its headline wording overstates the described tests, the results should be verified against a Nimbus or Blue Origin primary release before use.

key_values.tests_reported: launch-like vibration and shock (as described in the dek)

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the Apollo flight units in the sources reviewed. The ESA, Honda and Nimbus sources do not state dimensions for their fuel cell systems.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for any example. NASA states only that fuel cells offered more energy per pound than batteries over a long mission [1]. The Honda 'up to 10 kW' figure refers to a solar array, not the fuel cell [5].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for any fuel cell example in the sources reviewed. The Apollo fuel cell output values seen only in secondary summaries were not adopted. The Honda study gives no fuel cell power figure [5].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar surface presents a long night, low temperatures, a vacuum and dust. Press reporting on the Honda study describes a lunar night of about two weeks, with temperatures that can drop to -424 °F in some regions [5]. Fuel cell and electrolyser stacks need thermal management, both to keep the electrochemistry within its operating range and to reject heat. Reactant storage requires pressure control, insulation and leak management. The Apollo 13 incident showed the consequences of a reactant-tank failure [3]. Regenerative systems also require water handling and a daytime power source to drive electrolysis. These are engineering considerations drawn from the systems above. The publicly reviewed sources do not provide a qualified environmental requirement set for any named lunar fuel cell.
article.limitations: The concept has several limitations. A fuel cell system depends on reactant storage, and a tank or valve failure can remove generating capacity. The Apollo 13 service module incident is an example [3]. Regenerative systems add an electrolyser, which increases mass and complexity and introduces energy losses. None of the development examples reviewed provides a verified round-trip efficiency, mass-to-energy ratio, lifetime or lunar surface demonstration. Because the catalogue entry describes a category rather than one instrument, performance values from different systems cannot be compared without assumptions that the sources do not support.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Apollo fuel cells were not deployed separately. They were integrated into the Apollo service module, launched with the spacecraft and used for electrical power during the mission [1][3]. A surface regenerative system would be a different class of hardware. No delivery vehicle, lander or deployment method has been verified for any of the four examples reviewed.
transportation_process: Earth integration: qualify the reactant tanks and stacks, perform leak and pressure testing, and define safe handling procedures for hydrogen and oxygen.
Launch and lunar transfer: tolerate launch vibration and shock. The Nimbus test campaign is reported to have examined these loads [6].
Landing and surface deployment: provide mechanical mounting, thermal interfaces, and power and data connections to the host system.
Daytime energy source: a solar array or other source is needed to drive regeneration. The Honda study is an example of a solar-array-based integration concept [5].
Verification: confirm each interface against a named lander or host spacecraft. These are integration considerations, not verified interface requirements.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo fuel cells were installed in the service module and were not deployed on the lunar surface. Any surface regenerative system would require mechanical mounting, thermal and power interfaces, and a daytime energy source. No deployment method has been verified for the development examples.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo command and service module fuel cell power plants are the documented flight example. The ESA, Honda and Nimbus efforts are development, study or qualification examples and have not flown.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The ESA article suggests possible scale-up relevance to the Argonaut lunar lander, and the Honda study concerns Astrobotic's LunaGrid [4][5]. Neither source provides verified interface specifications. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo fuel cell power plants are the most important documented flight precedent. NASA credits the programme with helping to launch the commercial fuel cell industry [1]. NASA also states that it began investing in fuel cell technology in the 1960s [2]. Apollo 13 demonstrated both the value of redundant fuel cells and their dependence on shared reactant tanks [3]. The newer ESA, Honda and Nimbus efforts show a shift toward regenerative and solar-coupled energy storage for the lunar night. As of this review, they are development, study or qualification activities rather than flight-proven lunar systems [4][5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- The catalogue name is generic. This article covers a class of fuel cell applications, not one identified flight instrument.
- Apollo fuel cell power output, mass, dimensions and reactant handling were not confirmed from a primary technical document in this review. Values seen only in secondary search summaries were not adopted.
- The Apollo 13 account relies on a popular-history article [3]. The primary NASA investigation was not checked in this review.
- The ESA article is dated 2023 and reports results without a test location, measured performance or mission identification [4].
- The Honda study is an announced agreement, not a hardware programme [5].
- The Nimbus result is a secondary report with truncated text [6].
- Regenerative round-trip efficiency, specific energy, mass, lifetime and reliability are not verified for any development example.
- No verified direct image asset was identified for this payload, so the article contains no images.
